summary: The far north-western corner of Canada: the unglaciated British Mountains of the Yukon running down to the Beaufort Sea, with part of the calving grounds of the Porcupine caribou herd between them. Raft the Firth River through its canyons to the Arctic Ocean, or fly into the Inuvialuit-hosted base camp at Sheep Creek. About a hundred people come in a year, and charter aircraft from Inuvik are the practical way in.
story: The ice sheets of the last glacial period never reached the British Mountains, which take up about two-thirds of Ivvavik. They were part of Beringia, the ice-free land that reached across a bridge to Siberia and sheltered plants, animals and people while the rest of Canada lay under ice. That is why the land looks the way it does: V-shaped valleys, lone conical hills and rock towers called tors, shaped by frost, wind and water rather than glaciers. It is also why Parks Canada calls the Firth River the oldest flowing river in Canada.

Ivvavik means 'a place for giving birth, a nursery' in Inuvialuktun, and the name is for the Porcupine caribou, which migrate each year from the forested valleys of the north-central Yukon to calve on the coastal plain. Grizzly bears range across the whole park; black bears live here too, and polar bears come ashore on the coast, mostly in winter. Muskoxen keep to the coastal plain, and Dall's sheep reach the northern limit of their range in these mountains. The Firth carries one of the largest stocks of Dolly Varden char in western Canada.

People have lived here for a very long time. Sites along the Firth have produced projectile points 8,000 years old, and Engigstciak, a hill rising from the coastal plain, is the oldest known site in the park. Eight different cultures are known to have used the area. The Thule people arrived from Alaska about 1,100 years ago, and their descendants are the Inuvialuit, who built driftwood and sod houses along the coast. American whalers operated from Herschel Island from the mid-1880s, fur traders followed, and in the Cold War the first northern DEW Line radar site went up at Komakuk Beach.

In the 1970s oil and gas finds on the Alaskan North Slope and under the Beaufort Sea brought plans for a pipeline across the caribou's range, and Justice Thomas Berger's Mackenzie Valley Pipeline Inquiry called for an international wildlife refuge. The Inuvialuit wanted the land protected from development, and the Inuvialuit Final Agreement of 1984 set aside 9,750 square kilometres for a national park, the first in Canada created through an Indigenous land claim agreement. Parks Canada and the Inuvialuit manage it together, with the Wildlife Management Advisory Council (North Slope).
howItWorks: There are no roads into Ivvavik, and every trip starts at the Parks Canada office in Inuvik, Northwest Territories, 200 kilometres east of the park. Registration before entering and de-registration afterwards are mandatory for every visitor, researcher and anyone else going in, and failing to do so is an offence under the Canada National Parks Act. Registration includes a compulsory orientation, in which staff go over hazards, route conditions, water levels, closures, regulations and bear safety; you give your group's names, emergency contacts, equipment, itinerary and the date you will de-register. If you have not de-registered within 48 hours of that date, park staff start a search. A Superintendent's order makes all entry and travel in Ivvavik a restricted activity that needs a permit.

Charter aircraft from Inuvik are the most common and practical way in. The air access points are Margaret Lake, Imniarvik (Sheep Creek), Stokes Point, Nunaluk Spit and Komakuk Beach; the landing strips are not maintained, and some need special landing gear. No aircraft may land without a free Parks Canada Aircraft Landing Permit, which is issued when you register, and the charter company must also hold a National Parks Business Licence. Outfitted Firth River trips include the charter flight; for the base-camp trip the flight is booked for the group and its cost shared. In winter the park can be reached by ski-equipped aircraft, but snowmobiles may go only as far as the boundary.

Ivvavik has black bears, grizzlies and polar bears, and grizzlies are the ones visitors usually see. Every orientation includes a bear safety briefing with Parks Canada's film and its brochures on bear country and polar bear country; carry bear spray and an air horn, cook and store food at least 50 metres from your tents in bear-proof containers, and report any polar bear or its signs to the Duty Officer at once. Firearms may not be carried in the park. Fees are charged at registration: in November 2026 Parks Canada listed the Northern Park Backcountry Excursion/Camping permit at $37 per person per night or $259 for a year, valid in ten northern parks. Inuvialuit beneficiaries may harvest in the park under the Inuvialuit Final Agreement.

sights.name: Firth River
sights.note: About 130 navigable kilometres from Margaret Lake to the Beaufort Sea, through a succession of canyons with Class IV rapids. Rafted over one or two weeks.

sights.name: Imnairvik (Sheep Creek Base Camp)
sights.note: Parks Canada's camp beside the Firth at Sheep Creek: prospector tents inside an electric bear fence, an Inuvialuit cultural host, and day hikes to tors such as Wolf Tors and Halfway to Heaven.

sights.name: Engigstciak
sights.note: A hill rising from the coastal plain near the Firth, used by hunters to scan the land for thousands of years and the oldest known site in the park.

sights.name: British Mountains
sights.note: Never glaciated, they fill about two-thirds of the park, with ridges and peaks from 860 to 1,680 metres that grow more rugged towards the west.

sights.name: Nunaluk Spit
sights.note: Where Firth River trips end, on the Beaufort Sea. The one place in the park where wood fires are allowed, in Parks Canada's fire pits or a fire pan, with driftwood only.

sights.name: Komakuk Beach
sights.note: An air access point on the coast, and the site of the first northern DEW Line station, built by the American army in the 1950s.

sights.name: Stokes Point (Iqpiqyuuq)
sights.note: A coastal air access point for hikers, with the eroded remains of Inuvialuit camps and houses and the site of a later DEW Line station.

sights.name: Clarence Lagoon (Qaininqvik)
sights.note: A lagoon near the Alaska border where a trading post stood at the turn of the twentieth century; the remains of camps, graves and houses survive on its shore.

entrances: By charter aircraft from Inuvik, NT, about 200 kilometres east, to Margaret Lake, Imniarvik (Sheep Creek), Stokes Point, Nunaluk Spit or Komakuk Beach
In winter by ski-equipped aircraft; snowmobiles only as far as the park boundary
planYourVisit.reservations: Every trip must be registered at the Parks Canada office in Inuvik, with a mandatory orientation, and de-registered at the end. Places on the independent Imnairvik (Sheep Creek Base Camp) trip are booked by email with the Inuvik office; for 2026 registration opened on 20 February and the trip ran from 20 to 26 June. Check dates with Parks Canada before you go.
permits: Entry and travel permit, issued at registration; all travel in the park is a restricted activity
Aircraft Landing Permit, free, issued at registration; no aircraft may land without one
National Park Fishing Permit from the Inuvik office; Yukon licences are not valid
Permits for food or fuel caches, commercial filming and photography, and research
camping: No designated campsites: camp anywhere except at archaeological sites; Parks Canada has identified suitable sites along the Firth River
Tents in a line rather than a circle, at least 5 metres apart, with food stored and cooked at least 50 metres away
Wood fires only at Nunaluk Spit
lodging: Imnairvik (Sheep Creek Base Camp): prospector tents, kitchen, showers and flush toilets inside an electric bear fence, on Parks Canada's scheduled trip
Hotels and services in Inuvik; a year-round lodge in Aklavik
seasonalClosures: Winter-like conditions from mid-September to mid-May; the Inuvik office, where you register, keeps summer hours from 6 May to 13 September — check before you go

weather: Summer is short and changeable. Temperatures average 14°C and usually lie between 5°C and 25°C, but snow and frosts down to -15°C can come even in summer, and strong, long-lasting winds are common, so tents must be sturdy. The coast is cooled by the Beaufort Sea, whose pack ice can blow in at any time and brings fog; the centre and south of the park are drier with wider swings in temperature. Hiking runs from mid-June to mid-August: wildflowers peak in late June and early July, insects are worst in July, and autumn colours come in the third week of August with the risk of winter-like conditions. Winter averages -29°C, with a month of darkness.
directions: Inuvik, on the Mackenzie River in the Northwest Territories, is the starting point. Drive the Dempster Highway from Whitehorse, or fly in on one of the daily flights from southern Canada (Air North and Canadian North serve Inuvik). From Inuvik a charter aircraft or helicopter makes the 200-kilometre flight to the park; Aklavik, 55 kilometres from Inuvik and 150 from Ivvavik, has daily flights from Inuvik, but charters to the park still leave from Inuvik. Once dropped off, you are on your own until the plane returns, and weather often delays pick-ups: carry extra food and allow at least two spare days. Crossing into Alaska on foot, by river or by private aircraft needs prior clearance from Canadian and US border authorities.

fees.title: Northern Park Backcountry Excursion/Camping
fees.detail: $259.00 per person for a year, valid in Aulavik, Auyuittuq, Ivvavik, Nahanni, Quttinirpaaq, Sirmilik, Tuktut Nogait, Vuntut, Qausuittuq and Ukkusiksalik. Charged at registration. As listed by Parks Canada in November 2026; check before you go.

fees.title: National Park Fishing Permit
fees.detail: $76.50 for a year, from the Parks Canada office in Inuvik. As listed in November 2026.

fees.title: Imnairvik (Sheep Creek Base Camp) independent trip, 2026
fees.detail: Remote facility use, the backcountry permit and accommodation for the seven-day trip; the shared charter flight was estimated at a further $2,000 per person. Meals not included. Parks Canada's 2026 price.

chronology.text: Hunters leave projectile points along the Firth River; Engigstciak is in use.
The Thule people spread east from Alaska; their descendants are the Inuvialuit.
Alexander Mackenzie makes the first written records of the Inuvialuit.
American whalers begin operating from Herschel Island, just off the coast.
A small gold rush on the Firth River: about 200 claims are staked.
A placer mine opens at Sheep Creek; it runs until 1986, when Parks Canada buys it.
The Inuvialuit Final Agreement creates the park, the first in Canada set up through an Indigenous land claim agreement.
A new management plan for Ivvavik is tabled in Parliament in October.

safety: Ivvavik is one of the most isolated parks in North America. Rescue depends on weather, aircraft and staff and can take one to two days or more. Carry a satellite phone, SPOT or inReach: there is no mobile coverage.
Bears of all three species live here. Travel in groups, make noise in shrubby valley bottoms, carry bear spray and an air horn, and leave at once if you find a large carcass.

The Firth River can double in volume within hours after rain. Be ready to move camp to higher ground, and judge carefully before entering the canyon in high water. Never try to cross the Firth without a boat.
Aufeis, sheets of ice up to five metres thick, lies at the river's headwaters and delta. Stay clear of channels running under it and of undercut, overhanging edges.
Muskoxen and moose can charge, especially as the rut begins in late July. Keep your distance, ideally with a ravine, pond or creek between you.
regulations: Register before entering and de-register after; all travel in the park needs a permit.
No recreational drones: flying one can bring a fine of up to $25,000.
No firearms. No wood fires except at Nunaluk Spit, and only driftwood found on the ground there may be burned.
Parties on the Firth River must travel with at least two watercraft, and dogs are not allowed at Ivvavik Base Camp.
Fishing only with a National Park Fishing Permit: one Dolly Varden char and three fish in all per day, with several areas, among them the Firth River fish holes, closed to angling.
